input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-631: Foundations of Computer Vision. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: An introduction to the underlying concepts of computer vision and image understanding. The course will consider fundamental topics, including image formation, edge detection, texture analysis, color, segmentation, shape analysis, detection of objects in images and high level image representation. Depending on the interest of the class, more advanced topics will be covered, such as image database retrieval or robotic vision. Programming assignments are an integral part of the course. Note: students who complete CSCI-431 may not take CSCI-631 for credit. Prerequisites:(CSCI-603 and CSCI-605 and CSCI-661 with grades of B or better) or ((CSCI-243 or SWEN-262) and (CSCI-262 or CSCI-263)) or equiv courses. If earned credit for/or currently enrolled in CSCI-431 you will not be permitted to enroll in CSCI-631. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

Source excerpts:

[mit-computer-vision]
Computer vision connects image evidence to models of geometry, appearance, motion, objects, and scenes. Projective geometry relates three-dimensional points to image coordinates. Appearance models describe how lighting, material, and viewpoint affect measured pixels. Motion estimation compares observations across frames. Object recognition maps visual evidence to object hypotheses. Scene understanding combines objects, layout, and contextual relationships. A rigorous pipeline states the task, representation, assumptions, supervision, and decision rule. Evaluation tests sensitivity to viewpoint, lighting, occlusion, and data shift.

[opencv-documentation]
Computer vision pipelines represent images as numeric arrays. Color conversion changes the coordinate representation of pixel values. Filtering combines neighboring samples to smooth, sharpen, or detect structure. Feature methods locate and describe repeatable image patterns. Calibration estimates camera parameters needed for geometric measurement. Geometric transforms map coordinates between image representations. Segmentation assigns pixels or regions to selected categories. Motion methods compare observations across time. Results depend on sampling, illumination, noise, training data, thresholds, and evaluation metrics.

[rit-csci-631]
An introduction to the underlying concepts of computer vision and image understanding. The course will consider fundamental topics, including image formation, edge detection, texture analysis, color, segmentation, shape analysis, detection of objects in images and high level image representation. Depending on the interest of the class, more advanced topics will be covered, such as image database retrieval or robotic vision. Programming assignments are an integral part of the course. Note: students who complete CSCI-431 may not take CSCI-631 for credit. Prerequisites:(CSCI-603 and CSCI-605 and CSCI-661 with grades of B or better) or ((CSCI-243 or SWEN-262) and (CSCI-262 or CSCI-263)) or equiv courses. If earned credit for/or currently enrolled in CSCI-431 you will not be permitted to enroll in CSCI-631. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

beats.claim: Computer vision pipelines systematically transform raw image data into structured geometric and semantic models through a defined sequence of representation, assumptions, and rules
beats.example: A standard pipeline converts a raw camera image into a coordinate system, applies lighting models, extracts features, and outputs object hypotheses.
beats.title: Pipeline Architecture Overview
beats.visualDirection: Display a horizontal flowchart with five labeled stages: image acquisition, representation, assumption setting, supervision, and decision rule application.

beats.claim: Projective geometry mathematically relates three-dimensional scene points to two-dimensional image coordinates to enable accurate spatial measurement
beats.example: A camera lens maps a three-dimensional object's vertices to specific pixel locations using a projection matrix that accounts for focal length and sensor position.
beats.title: Image Formation & Geometry
beats.visualDirection: Show a diagram of a camera projecting 3D world points onto a 2D image plane using perspective lines and a focal point marker.

beats.claim: Appearance models describe how lighting, material properties, and viewpoint changes affect measured pixel values across different conditions
beats.example: A matte surface reflects ambient light uniformly, while a glossy surface creates specular highlights that shift with the camera angle.
beats.title: Appearance Modeling
beats.visualDirection: Display a split image showing the same object under two different lighting conditions and camera angles, highlighting pixel value variations.

beats.claim: Motion estimation compares observations across consecutive frames to calculate displacement and track object trajectories over time
beats.example: A video sequence of a moving car is analyzed by aligning corresponding pixels between frames to compute velocity vectors and path trajectories.
beats.title: Motion Estimation
beats.visualDirection: Show a side-by-side frame comparison with overlaid displacement arrows indicating pixel movement between consecutive video frames.

beats.claim: Object recognition maps visual evidence to object hypotheses by matching extracted features against learned class signatures
beats.example: A system identifies a traffic sign by comparing edge patterns and color distributions in the image to a database of known sign templates.
beats.title: Object Recognition
beats.visualDirection: Display a bounding box around a detected object with a confidence score and a list of matched class hypotheses below the box.

beats.claim: Scene understanding combines detected objects, spatial layout, and contextual relationships to form a coherent interpretation of the visual environment
beats.example: A street scene is interpreted by recognizing a pedestrian, a road, and a building, then assigning semantic relationships such as 'standing on' and 'adjacent to'.
beats.title: Scene Understanding
beats.visualDirection: Show a labeled scene graph with nodes representing objects and edges indicating spatial and contextual relationships between them.

beats.claim: Computer vision pipelines represent images as numeric arrays that enable efficient computation and transformation through standardized coordinate systems
beats.example: A color image is converted from RGB to HSV space to isolate luminance information from chromatic variations for better edge detection.
beats.title: Image Representation & Conversion
beats.visualDirection: Display a color bar showing the RGB to HSV conversion process, with a side-by-side comparison of the original and converted image channels.

beats.claim: Filtering combines neighboring samples to smooth, sharpen, or detect structure, while feature methods locate and describe repeatable image patterns
beats.example: A Gaussian filter smooths a noisy image to reduce high-frequency noise, and a SIFT detector extracts scale-invariant keypoints for matching.
beats.title: Filtering & Feature Extraction
beats.visualDirection: Show a before-and-after image pair demonstrating noise reduction and a heatmap overlay highlighting detected feature keypoints.

beats.claim: Segmentation assigns pixels or regions to selected categories, and shape analysis characterizes object boundaries and structural properties
beats.example: A binary mask isolates a vehicle from a background, and contour approximation algorithms reduce the boundary to a polygon for further analysis.
beats.title: Segmentation & Shape Analysis
beats.visualDirection: Display a segmented image with color-coded regions and a simplified polygon overlay representing the object's shape.

beats.claim: Evaluation tests sensitivity to viewpoint, lighting, occlusion, and data shift to verify that vision systems maintain accuracy under varying conditions
beats.example: A detection model is tested across different camera angles and lighting levels to measure false positive rates and localization error.
beats.title: Evaluation & Robustness
beats.visualDirection: Show a confusion matrix and a heatmap of detection accuracy across different environmental conditions like lighting and occlusion levels.

learningObjectives: Define the core components of a computer vision pipeline and explain how they transform raw image data into structured geometric and semantic models.
Apply fundamental image processing techniques, including color conversion, filtering, and feature extraction, to analyze visual patterns and lighting,
Evaluate the impact of environmental factors such as viewpoint, illumination, and occlusion on vision system performance and accuracy.

Consider this worked case: A street scene is interpreted by recognizing a pedestrian, a road, and a building, then assigning semantic relationships such as 'standing on' and 'adjacent to'. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost.

Apply Object Recognition to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. Object recognition maps visual evidence to object hypotheses. Consider this worked case: A system identifies a traffic sign by comparing edge patterns and color distributions in the image to a database of known sign templates. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it.

With the foundation in place, examine how Appearance Modeling operates in a concrete sequence. Appearance models describe how lighting, material, and viewpoint affect measured pixels. Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence.

Use Filtering & Feature Extraction to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. Filtering combines neighboring samples to smooth, sharpen, or detect structure.
